Executive Workforce Analysis

C-SUITE BRIEFING — SYNTHESIZED FROM 17,414 EMPLOYEE RECORDS

🟢 Growth Signals

SIGNAL 1Referred hires dramatically outperform. Employees recruited through referrals achieve a 53.2% KPI rate — nearly double the 35.6% average across all channels. This is the single highest-ROI hiring lever available and it is barely used (only 1.8% of hires come from referrals).

SIGNAL 2R&D and Operations punch above their weight. R&D (44.9% KPI rate) and Operations (44.1%) consistently outperform the company average of 35.9%, despite R&D being the smallest headcount department. These teams are the performance backbone of the organization.

SIGNAL 3Below Secondary education workers outperform on KPIs. Surprisingly, employees with below-secondary education achieve a 46.5% KPI rate — the highest of any education group. This signals strong on-the-job performance in operational and hands-on roles.

🔴 Leakage Signals

RISK 1Training investment is being wasted at scale. 1,985 employees (11.4% of the workforce) scored 80+ on training assessments but still failed to meet KPIs. This is a clear disconnect between learning input and performance output — and a direct cost to the L&D budget.

RISK 2Recognition is broken. 3,696 employees received a 5-star performance rating last year but won zero awards. This recognition gap is a retention time bomb — your best performers feel invisible.

RISK 3Sales & Marketing is a silent crisis. With 5,458 employees (31% of the workforce), Sales & Marketing has the lowest KPI achievement rate at just 27.7% — nearly 10 points below the company average. This is not a small team with minor underperformance; it is the largest department, and it is failing at its core metric.

Overall Workforce Health Assessment

Score: 5.8 / 10 — Structurally sound, operationally fragile. The organization has 17,414 people with an average age of 34.8 years — a relatively young, potentially high-energy workforce. Average tenure of 5.8 years suggests neither alarming turnover nor dangerous stagnation. But a 35.9% KPI achievement rate means that nearly two-thirds of employees are not hitting their targets in any given year. That is a workforce operating at roughly one-third capacity on its primary performance metric. The average training score of 63.2 out of 100 shows moderate learning engagement, but training is not converting into performance outcomes — the correlation between training count and KPI achievement is actually negative, meaning more training sessions are being assigned to underperformers without a remediation strategy.

The single most important action management should take: Fix the referral pipeline and fix Sales & Marketing — in that order. Doubling down on referral hiring could shift the KPI baseline by 15+ points within 18 months. Simultaneously, Sales & Marketing needs a diagnostic intervention: identify whether underperformance is a target-setting problem, a people problem, or a process problem. With 5,458 people at 27.7% KPI attainment, even a 5-point improvement in that department would move the company's overall KPI rate from 35.9% to approximately 38.5% — the equivalent of adding 450 high performers overnight.

Hidden star: R&D Smallest team, highest KPI rate (44.9%), punching well above its weight. Hidden risk: Sales & Marketing Largest team, lowest KPI rate, 81% male, highest gender concentration imbalance. The organization's biggest headcount investment is also its weakest performance engine.
